items.title: After a $2.5 Trillion Wipeout, Tech Investors Brace for More Pain
items.summary: A stock rally fueled in part by artificial intelligence is being tested after Democrats’ landslide election victories.

items.title: Here’s the latest.
items.full_text: Gena Pemberton is a Black woman who has spent her career diagnosing a way to move forward in corporate America. She spent over two decades in leadership roles in accounting, operations and human resources at large companies such as Johnson & Johnson. But now, at 50, she is not sure what is next. “We really do just remain in this low-hire, low-fire environment,” said Laura Ullrich, the director of economic research at Indeed, the job search website. The stability has allowed consumers to keep spending, buoying the economy overall. But for those without jobs, opportunities have been more limited. And even people who do have jobs have been losing leverage, as wage growth has slowed and inflation has eroded their spending power . Here’s what to watch in the report: New vigor? There have been some tentative signs that the labor market may be perking up. The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey this week showed that the quits rate rose in September, a sign that workers may feel more confident in their ability to get new jobs. But broadly, the labor market picture has not shifted much. A.I.’s fingerprints: One big question hanging over the labor market is the impact of artificial intelligence. So far, the technology does not appear to be leading to widespread job losses despite some recent layoff announcements from big companies including Microsoft. Trouble spots: At the same time, there are some indications that the rise of the technology is depressing hiring, particularly for entry-level positions in sectors including financial services and information. Part of the reason may be that employers are holding off on hiring as they assess A.I.’s capabilities. Companies may also be choosing to invest in A.I. rather than adding employees. A.I. may even be fueling hiring in sectors tied to the data center buildout, including construction. The labor market has not contributed to the inflation problem confronting the Fed, a dynamic expected to be affirmed when data for October is released on Friday. Monthly jobs growth has bounced around, but the unemployment rate has remained stable, at 4.2 percent, and wage growth has been subdued. This backdrop is a welcome one for policymakers at the Fed. It suggests they can afford to focus primarily on curbing inflation, which has overshot the central bank’s 2 percent target for nearly six years. The primary drivers of inflation include the war with Iran, which has unleashed an energy shock that has sharply lifted oil prices, as well as a spending boom by technology companies building out their artificial intelligence abilities. Shares in those companies have come under pressure after Democrats’ sweeping victory in this week’s midterm elections that gave them firm control of both chambers of Congress. The prospects of heightened A.I. scrutiny and a regulatory crackdown prompted a steep slide in U.S. stocks, with the S&P 500 notching its worst daily decline on Thursday in more than a year. Fed officials are tracking gyrations in the stock market and the trajectory of U.S. government bond yields, which together influence the availability of credit in the economy. Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed chairman, acknowledged at the bank’s policy meeting last week that those financial conditions had become tighter. But he said he was “unwilling and unable to call them tight.” Mr. Warsh appeared to welcome the move, saying that it helped “in the direction of achieving a longer, more durable period of economic growth and price stability.” Mr. Warsh made clear that the Fed’s goal wasn’t “to throw sand in the gears of the economy and throw people out of work.” That suggests the bar is relatively high for the Fed to jettison its gradual approach to raising rates. It would take fresh evidence that price pressures are intensifying, and perhaps beginning to stem from the labor market. That would very likely necessitate a much more aggressive response from the Fed, either in terms of the pace of further rate increases or the total amount it would eventually deliver. Futures for the S&P 500 signaled that the benchmark index would rise slightly when official trading opens in New York. The Nasdaq, which was at the forefront of the rout on Thursday, was set to open more than 1 percent higher, driven by a bounce in chip makers, like Nvidia. A rally on Friday would continue the week’s wrenching volatility, which saw stocks rise as the U.S. midterm election results rolled in, but then veer sharply lower as investors grappled with the prospects for the A.I. investment boom after the Democrats’ landslide victory. The shift in power in Congress led many analysts to suggest that stricter regulation of data centers could slow growth in states where the world’s largest tech companies are aggressively building out computing capacity. Phillip Wool, head of research and portfolio management at Rayliant, an investment firm, said that even if a Congress controlled by Democrats wanted to take a tougher approach on A.I. companies, President Trump still held veto power. “At best, this is probably a stalemate, and it’s just going to bring more attention to some of the risks of A.I.,” he said. Other market watchers said that the sell-off most likely represented traders resetting their positions as they assessed the implications of the U.S. elections, rather than an end to the A.I. investment cycle that had propelled markets higher for much of this year. “While we could see a period of market indigestion following the election results, we do not think fundamentals justify a prolonged downturn,” said Mark Haefele, the chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, adding that corporate earnings remained resilient. But he warned that more spells of market volatility could be ahead. The latest U.S. jobs report, due before the market opens on Friday, typically moves markets and will be another factor attracting investors’ attention. Markets across Asia, which were closed during the worst of the selling on Wall Street, had a chaotic open to trading on Friday. The severity of the initial selling in South Korea triggered a 20-minute trading halt at the exchange in Seoul. The tech-heavy KOSPI plunged 6 percent by the end of the session, pulled down by the memory chip makers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 sank about 6 percent, dropping the index into a bear market, defined as a 20 percent fall from its recent peak. Shares of SoftBank, a major investor in OpenAI and a proxy for investor sentiment on A.I., plunged 11 percent. In Europe, the Stoxx 600, a broad index that tracks the region’s largest companies, shed more than 1 percent. All of the continent’s major markets, in Frankfurt, Paris, London and beyond, posted declines, but the moves were less severe than elsewhere, since European indexes are less influenced by technology companies. In fact, some of Europe’s biggest tech companies posted gains on Friday. ASML, Infineon and STMicroelectronics were among the stocks that rose between 2 and 4 percent. For Mohit Kumar, a strategist at Jefferies, the recent turmoil after the U.S. midterms was not a sign of the unwinding of the A.I. trade. “One could argue that having more guardrails makes A.I. investment more sustainable in the medium term,” he wrote in a research note. For years, Microsoft occupied a distinct position among the tech industry’s biggest companies. While its pay packages often lagged behind Silicon Valley rivals like Google and Meta, employees said, the company countered with strong benefits and a reputation for stability. As recently as September, Forbes ranked Microsoft the world’s best employer for the third straight year. But the tech industry’s A.I. race is upending many workplaces, Microsoft included. The buyout offer, said six Microsoft employees who spoke on the condition of anonymity, landed on workers strained by mounting expectations to use A.I., stagnant pay and a growing sense that their jobs were no longer secure. Though Microsoft is doing better financially than most of its peers, it is clearly shifting its spending priorities. Two days after the buyouts were announced, the Redmond, Wash., company reported a 32 percent jump in quarterly profit, to $36.6 billion, on revenue of $92.3 billion. Its capital spending, largely on data centers, rose 30 percent to $45.2 billion, and the company said it expected to spend roughly $170 billion this year. The fear among many workers now is what comes next, and some have begun organizing. Before the buyout offer, a group of current and former employees circulated an open letter among colleagues accusing the company of pursuing A.I. with a “speed-at-all-costs” ethos. It called on Microsoft to involve employees in decisions about how A.I. is built and used, and to stop tying A.I. use to rewards or reprimands. Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s executive vice president and chief people officer, said the buyouts were meant to give employees who might be ready for something new “choice and agency.” She said the buyouts were not related to how A.I. was changing work. (A Microsoft spokeswoman said “maintenance timing,” rather than a traffic surge, had briefly delayed the release of some buyout offers on the internal site.) Ms. Coleman also did not rule out future layoffs. Employees offered a buyout have until Dec. 9 to decide, and those who accept will leave on Dec. 31. They will receive a minimum of eight weeks of base pay, and the size of the payment varies by job level and tenure. The offer followed a string of cuts that had already shaken employees. Microsoft laid off 10,000 workers in 2023, and more than 15,000 in 2025. This spring, about 8,600 U.S. employees were offered a retirement-age buyout, and about 30 percent accepted it. This summer, the company cut about 4,800 more jobs. Microsoft’s head count in June was 223,000, down 5,000 from a year earlier. Microsoft’s campus in Redmond, Wash.
